Writing a Discord bot in Rust for no reason

There are two kinds of side projects: the ones that solve a problem, and the ones where the language is the problem you wanted. This was the second kind.

The bot does one thing: it posts in our server when a new episode of whatever we’re watching airs. A cron job and a webhook could do this in eleven lines of Python. Instead I have a tokio runtime, a typed command framework, and opinions about serde.

#[command]
async fn airing(ctx: Context<'_>) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let next = schedule::next_episode().await?;
    ctx.say(format!("{} airs in {}", next.title, next.eta)).await?;
    Ok(())
}

Was it worth it? The bot has never crashed, which is more than I can say for the eleven-line Python version it replaced. The compiler and I are friends now. This is how they get you.
What Dungeon Meshi taught me about scope creep

Laios and party set out to rescue one person. By volume nine they're renegotiating the fundamental relationship between the dungeon's ecosystem and the surface world. This is the most accurate depiction of a side project I have ever seen.

Every project I start is "eat monsters to save Falin": a clear goal, a scrappy plan, and a budget of zero. Every project I'm still working on six months later has somehow become "restructure the dungeon."

The lesson isn't "don't expand scope." Senshi's whole philosophy is that you engage seriously with what's in front of you, and the party is better for it. The lesson is to expand scope *deliberately*, one meal at a time, and to know which quest you're actually on.

Anyway, my anime notifier CLI now has a plugin system. I am aware of the irony.

Self-hosting my RSS reader was worth it

I finally moved off the hosted reader I'd been using since 2019. Partly for the usual self-hosting reasons, partly because I wanted my now-playing widget to pull from the same database. The setup is a single container behind a reverse proxy. Deploying it looked roughly like: ```yaml # docker-compose.yml services: miniflux: image: miniflux/miniflux:latest ``` > The best sync service is the one where you can read the sync code. Total migration time: one evening and two episodes of Frieren. No regrets so far. (´。• ᵕ •。`)

Nix, six months in: a love-hate letter

Six months ago I nuked my perfectly functional Arch install and rebuilt everything on NixOS. This is the retrospective I promised myself I'd write. The love: my entire system is a git repo. New machine? `nixos-rebuild switch --flake .` and twenty minutes later everything is exactly where I left it, down to the terminal padding. Rollbacks have saved me twice from my own enthusiasm. The hate: the documentation situation is still "read the source and squint," and error messages appear to be generated by an adversarial model. I keep a growing note of incantations in the garden because I will absolutely not remember them. > Nix is what happens when you solve a real problem so thoroughly that using the solution becomes its own hobby. Verdict: staying. But I understand every person who bounced off it. (￣ヘ￣)

Collecting vocabulary for why some pages read effortlessly and others fight you. Current notes:

Gutter width is pacing — wide gutters slow the eye, cramped ones accelerate. A bleed panel isn't "big for drama," it's a held breath; the story pauses while the image expands past time. Dungeon Meshi does dense 8-panel grids for comedy and then spends a full page on a single meal, and the contrast *is* the joke.

Want to explore next: how [[games-as-teaching]] overlaps — tutorial design and panel flow are both invisible-when-good.

The mental model that finally made Docker networking stop feeling like spellcasting:

- Every compose project gets its own bridge network; containers resolve each other by service name.
- Published ports are NAT rules on the host, nothing more.
- "Why can't the container reach the host?" — use the gateway IP, or `host.docker.internal` where supported.

Most of my self-hosting problems (see [[rss-everything]]) turn out to be DNS. It's always DNS.

The motions that actually changed how I edit, as opposed to the ones I learned for party tricks:

- `ci(` / `ci"` — change inside delimiters. The gateway drug.
- `.` — repeat. The whole editing model clicks when you start composing for repeatability.
- `%` — jump between matching pairs. Free with no config.
- `g;` — jump to last change. Criminally under-taught.

Everything below is pinned via [[nix-flakes]], so my neovim config is identical on every machine — which is the only reason muscle memory like this survives.

How this site is built, for the three people who will ask:

- **Framework**: Astro — static output, components where they help, zero client JS by default.
- **Theme**: Catppuccin, same as everything else I own (see [[dotfiles-philosophy]]) — Mocha by default, Latte for the daylight people. Toggle is in the header.
- **Type**: JetBrains Mono for everything. Yes, everything. It's my site.
- **Hosting**: a small VPS behind the same reverse proxy as the rest of my [[rss-everything]] stack.

Design principles: fast, boring, slightly weird. The 88×31 badges are load-bearing.
